body: The sheet of printer paper is still propped against the rail at the Marian shrine, but it isn’t blank under HAITI anymore. Since last night it has filled from the top down in ballpoint and Sharpie and one green crayon: first names, a town after some of them, a few with *mother* or *brother* in front. Near the bottom, in Kevin’s tidy printing, PIERRE (DOUG’S, BAND CAMP) — DELRAY.

The twelve-ten is usually eleven people and Mrs. Fitch. Today it is full to the side aisle, and the people at the back are standing in their coats. Fr. Osei comes out in the green. Before the opening prayer he says what the Mass is for, without ornament: for Joseph Serge Miot, Archbishop of Port-au-Prince, found this morning in the ruins of his offices, that he may rest in peace; and for everyone in that city who has not been found.

Joey Abruzzo, who has never read anything at less than the volume of a kickoff, reads the first reading quietly: a boy asleep in the temple who hears his name in the night, and goes to the old priest, and is sent back to bed, and hears it again. Kenzie sings the psalm without the piano, and the church sings the response back to her, ragged: *Here am I, Lord; I come to do your will.*

Osei reads the Gospel himself, standing straight to spare the leg, and when he comes to the last thing the disciples say he gives it no more weight than anything else in the chapter: *Everyone is looking for you.* The woman in the pew ahead of Jack puts her fingers against her mouth.

There is no homily. Osei comes down to the foot of the sanctuary step, where he stood last night, and says it with his hands folded. “Everyone in Port-au-Prince is calling a name into the dark tonight, and all I know to tell you is to pray that somebody answers, *Here I am*.” He goes back up to the altar.

For the intercessions Kenzie takes the sheet down from the rail and reads it through, name by name, as far as the paper goes. It takes four minutes. She reads PIERRE and then, because it says so, *band camp, Delray*, and the church answers him as it answers all of them.

body.text: When the line forms Jack goes up with it and receives, and comes back down the side aisle with his hands folded and the Host still dissolving on his tongue.
body.else: The line goes up past his knees and Jack stays where he is. He says the old prayer Nonna taught him, the second time since Monday, with his eyes on the driftwood crucifix, and gets as far as *come at least spiritually into my heart* when Kenzie starts the communion hymn over his head. It isn’t the same thing. It is what there is, and the line goes on without him.

body: Mrs. Fitch, in her lanyard, reads the announcements from the lectern as she reads them every day. The table on the Commons Lawn is open until five. Checks to Catholic Relief Services, not to Newman. Thursday night, nine to midnight, the chapel is open for a holy hour, which Tyler Brandt would like it known was his idea; Tyler Brandt, in the fourth pew, looks at his shoes and beams.
Afterward Osei is at the door under the bell, as he is every day, and he isn’t saying *Akwaaba* to anyone. When Jack reaches him he says it low, before Jack has opened his mouth.
“Yaw is alive,” Osei says. “He is operating in a parking lot.”
“Thank God.”
“I have been, since five this morning.”

body.text: Already turning to the next coat in line, Osei adds one more word. “Saturday.” Jack nods.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot.

s09.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:10 PM · THE COMMONS LAWN, UNDER FERRER TOWER — THE NEWMAN TABLE
body: The table is the one with four legs. Two sophomores carried it over from the Newman courtyard at nine and set it down on the only level stretch of the Commons Lawn that the sprinklers miss, under Ferrer Tower, and the fog burned off at noon, and by ten past one the table has the look of a thing that has been there for years: Lena’s sign taped across the front in purple marker, a gray cash box in the middle, a coffee can for coins, and in a webbed lawn chair at the end Mrs. Fitch, with a cooler at her feet and a paper plate of lemon bars under plastic wrap and an index card in her own hand that says $1.

body.title: A sign, hand-lettered, taped to the front of the table
body.text:
HAITI
CATHOLIC RELIEF SERVICES
CASH OR CHECKS (CHECKS TO CRS)

body: Peter Haddad, who has had the box since nine, hands it across with both hands and lets his shoulders down. The box never leaves the table, he says, and change never comes out of it; she will know. He is back at five for the bank bag. His MacBook stays behind, propped on the cooler with CNN.com on it and the sound off.
“Rule four,” Becca reads from the protocol card taped inside the lid, in Lena’s handwriting. “The box is never alone with one person.” She looks at Jack. “That’s us. We’re two.”

Becca is already in her place behind the cash box, in the St. Brendan’s Coffee & Donuts apron with the receipt book in the pocket and her clipboard squared on the table. She has her grandmother’s rosary wound twice around her wrist and her braid over one shoulder, and at her elbow a cigar box that rattles. “Change,” she says, and taps the lid. “Coins first. I made change for four hundred people at the Kootenai County Fair, and Lena says the box doesn’t make change, so I brought a box.”

body.text: “Did you eat?” She asks it the same as she does every Sunday at the Coffee and Donuts, looking at his face instead of his hands. “You didn’t. There’s a sandwich in my bag. It’s the heavy kind.”
“Thomas came out for a shrimp pellet this morning,” she says, “and took it back in with him. He is still not speaking to me.”
She bumps his shoulder with hers on her way past to the lemon bars, and goes on squaring the receipts.
“Hi, Jack!” She pushes the cigar box a few inches toward him. “You do the dollars. I’ll do the coins.”

body: It is lemon bars and dollars. A man from the dining hall in a hairnet puts five singles in the coffee can, one at a time, and goes back in to his shift. Two girls in Portolá sweatshirts put in a ten between them. A freshman tells Mrs. Fitch he can’t have a lemon bar because he’s allergic to lemons. “Then give Haiti a dollar,” Mrs. Fitch says, “and think about what you’ve done,” and he does. Becca writes each receipt in her round, careful hand, name and amount, and tears it off along the perforation, and gives it over with both hands. Ferrer Tower plays the quarter hour over their heads, a note or two flat.
“How’s your Nonna?” Becca asks, squaring the receipts.
“She lit a candle Tuesday and won’t say who for.”
“That’s allowed,” Becca says. “That’s the best kind. I’m on it.”

On the cooler, CNN.com has something it can show. A slope of broken concrete, men in shirtsleeves, a rope, and a woman being passed up out of a gap in it, hand to hand, into the daylight. She is alive. Jack can see her blink.

Becca stops with a quarter in each hand. “Look at her,” she says. “They got her. I put Haiti in my Glory Be at breakfast, and again at lunch. It fits anywhere. It’s short.” She turns her wrist, and the rosary swings. “This was my grandma’s. Agnes. She gave it to me when I left for here.”

“We drive over to Kellogg every May,” she says. “It’s forty minutes from us, in the Silver Valley, and Grandma brings a thermos. She sits and has her coffee, because Grandpa Walt’s name is on the memorial there.” She says it as information. “He was in the Sunshine Mine in ’seventy-two, when it caught fire. And Grandma went up to the gate with the other families, and she said this” — the wrist again — “at the gate for eight days. Eight days. And on the eighth day they brought two men up. Alive.”
“So you never stop,” Becca says. “That’s what she says. You just never stop.”
A boy with a skateboard wants a lemon bar and holds out a five. She makes his change out of the cigar box, coins first, and tells him God bless.

Jack has been banding the morning’s twenties since the thermos. His thumb goes through the same one twice. “That’s the same one,” Becca says, gently, not looking up from the receipt book. “Start the stack over. It’s the first rule of cash.” He starts the stack over. Under the plastic wrap Mrs. Fitch has stopped straightening the lemon bars.

response: He takes out his wallet and finds the twenty he has carried since Glenwood Avenue, folded small and square, still faintly butterscotch. He counts it once. He lays it in the box on top of the others, flat.
“That’s a lot,” Becca says. Her pen has stopped over the receipt book.
“It was for a trip.”
She looks at him, and then she writes it up. “Who do I put?”
“Carmela.”
CARMELA R., in the round careful hand, and *$20.00 — with thanks*. She tears it off and gives it to him with both hands, and he folds it into the wallet where the twenty was.

choices.text: “Pray it for them, Becca. Right now.”
response: “Okay,” Becca says. She doesn’t ask why, or whether it’s the right time. She unwinds the rosary from her wrist and starts it where she stands, the beads going through her fingers and her lips moving, straight behind the cash box with the clipboard under her arm.

Partway through the third Hail Mary two freshmen want lemon bars. She sells them both, makes their change, writes the receipts and hands them over, lips still moving, and does not lose her place. Jack comes in on the second half of each one, under his breath, and minds the box.

He says nothing. A man in a UPS-brown jacket with a hand truck stops for a lemon bar and holds out a ten, and Jack counts his change out of Becca’s cigar box the way his mother does at the St. Brigid’s bake sale: coins first, into the palm, the bills on top, so the hand feels the weight before it feels the paper.
“Thanks, man,” the man says, and walks off with a lemon bar in one hand and the change in the other, looking back at the laptop over his shoulder until the corner of the Brick takes him.

s15.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
body: He left his charger in the lounge outlet this morning, the only live one on four that Theo’s power strip doesn’t own, and at ten to eleven, with the RAZR down to its last bar, he goes up to get it.

There is light under the lounge door. Someone has taped a sheet of construction paper over the little wired window from the inside, and behind the paper Laney’s pink iPod dock on the sill is doing Lady Antebellum at a volume meant to cover talk rather than accompany it. His hand is on the handle when the song drops into its low part, and a voice comes through the door with nothing in the way.
“…the laptop’s in my closet, Theodore, and it’s staying there —”
He opens the door.

Every light is on. In the corner the vending machine hums its one note. Laney is cross-legged on the coffee table in the Pi Lam hoodie with a legal pad in her lap and index cards in three colors, turned over, fanned around her knees. Theo is on his feet in the rush blazer, one arm out, with his fingers still on the frame of the whiteboard — Margot’s, by annexation, on its wheeled stand — and it is still turning. It finishes a half-turn as Jack comes in and settles, and the side that faces him is hers: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, in her capitals, and under it COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD, over a column of her marks, months old and never wiped, because she says it’s a record. Priya’s laminate is still taped to the frame. The other side faces the wall.
“It is a whiteboard,” Margot says, from the armchair. “It is not a lazy Susan.”

“Costigan,” Theo says. “Good. We’re organizing a benefit.” His fingers haven’t left the frame. “For Haiti. Pi Lam and Sigma Rho, jointly, Friday the twenty-ninth, in the Pi Lam chapter room, doors at seven, capacity a hundred and twelve, per the fire marshal, who was consulted at four o’clock. A date auction. Silent for the first hour, live for the second, eleven lots, every dollar to Catholic Relief Services at Lena’s insistence. She’ll insist when she hears. Priya is drafting the waiver.” On the sill the song goes on to its next verse. “Kevin is our medical liaison. Margot is keeping the minutes. I’m lot nine.”

“Theodore’s being auctioned,” Laney says. She is reading it off the pad. “Lot four, a Sigma Rho who can cook. Lot six, a Pi Lam with a boat. Lot nine, Theodore, who comes with a quote.” She has not looked up. The pen in her hand has stopped on the last lot. The nails around it are red and blue, done for Haiti this afternoon, and the thumbnail has been chewed through the polish. On the table by her shoe there is a tray of Anacapa cheese cubes with toothpicks in them, untouched.

On the couch Kevin has his arms folded and his BlackBerry face-down on his knee. There is a Post-it on the front of his quarter-zip that says MEDICAL LIAISON in Theo’s hand. “Respectfully,” he says, before anyone has asked, “I was brought here.”
Margot has her Docs up on the table beside Laney’s knee and the notebook open on her own. “I’m taking notes,” she says. “For science. This is the sixth time through this song.”
“It’s helping,” Laney says.
Upside down from the door, across the top of her open page, there is one word in capitals: SKYE.

body.text: A Res Life flyer is folded into the gutter beside it with a line on it in Theo’s hand, upside down, and Jack can read it anyway: THE ROSE IS A PLANT.

body: “You said there would be a sandwich,” Kevin says to Theo.
“There is a sandwich,” Theo says, and indicates the cheese cubes with the tips of his fingers.
“That’s cheese.”
“It’s cheese-adjacent.”
“The minutes will reflect that Kevin objected,” Margot says.
“Thank you,” says Kevin.
“And that he stayed.”
Kevin looks at the ceiling. He stays.
The charger is in the outlet behind Kevin’s couch.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge: taking notes, for science. A page in her notebook says SKYE.

response: “I’m out of your price range, Costigan,” Theo says. “Bidding opens at a hundred and forty. I’ve been appraised.”
“By whom?” says Margot.
“A professional.”
Laney, to the ceiling: “*Lord.*”
He reaches behind the couch for the charger on his way out, and Kevin leans forward to let him.
“Night,” Laney says, without turning her head.
It is the first word she has said to him since Sunday. He says it back to the top of her head, and goes. In the hall behind him the casters start up on the carpet again, and the song starts over.

choices.text: “What’s on the other side of the board?”
response: “Data,” Margot says.
“Feelings,” says Kevin.
“*Kevin*,” Laney says.
“Logistics,” Theo says, a little late.
He reaches behind the couch for the charger on his way out, and Kevin leans forward to let him.
“Night,” Laney says, without turning her head.
It is the first word she has said to him since Sunday. He says it back to the top of her head, and goes. In the hall behind him the casters start up on the carpet again, and the song starts over.

choices.text: *Get your charger off the outlet and go.*
response: He goes around the end of the couch. The charger is where he left it, in the wall behind Kevin’s shoulder, and Kevin reaches back, pulls it out and hands it over without a word.
“Night,” Laney says, without turning her head.
It is the first word she has said to him since Sunday. He says it back to the top of her head, and goes. In the hall behind him the casters start up on the carpet again, and the song starts over.
